triage.name: Asthma in Children
triage.reason: Classic pediatric presentation with recurrent wheeze, cough and dyspnea; diagnosis reachable by history, exam and spirometry, with important look-alikes such as bronchiolitis and foreign body.

rule_errors: reply unusable: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 6244 (char 6243)
workup: 'spirometry with bronchodilator response' appears in ['initial', 'confirmatory']; use one group, or not_indicated plus one entry with only_if

demographics: More common in boys during childhood; the sex difference narrows or reverses in adolescence
Higher prevalence among Black and Puerto Rican children in the US
More common in children living in urban, low-income neighborhoods

risk_factors.text: Maternal smoking during pregnancy or secondhand smoke exposure in early childhood
Personal history of atopic dermatitis or allergic rhinitis
Frequent viral respiratory infections in early childhood

family_history: Asthma in a parent or sibling
Allergic rhinitis or atopic dermatitis in a parent or sibling
social_history: Exposure to secondhand smoke at home or in a caregiver's car
Living in older housing with dust mites, mold, or cockroaches
Attending daycare or school with frequent viral illnesses

chief_complaints.text: My child has been wheezing and coughing at night
He can't keep up with the other kids when playing
She has a whistling sound when she breathes out
He wakes up coughing and can't catch his breath

hpi.onset: Gradual over weeks to months, often starting in early childhood; individual flare-ups can come on over hours or suddenly
hpi.duration: Recurrent episodes over months to years; each flare-up lasts days to weeks if untreated
hpi.progression: Symptoms come and go, often worse at night and with triggers such as colds, exercise, or allergens; between episodes the child may be completely well
hpi.quality: Wheezing, cough, chest tightness, and shortness of breath
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; can be life-threatening during a severe attack
hpi.timing: Often worse at night or early morning; may be triggered by exercise, cold air, or viral infections

associated_symptoms.text: Cough, especially at night or early morning
Shortness of breath or rapid breathing
Trouble eating or sucking in infants

pertinent_negatives: Chest pain that is sharp and pleuritic
Choking episode or sudden onset while eating

argues_against: Gastroesophageal reflux disease as sole cause

positives.text: Known allergies to pets, dust, or pollen

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants may present with trouble feeding, rapid breathing, or coughing during feeds rather than classic wheezing; diagnosis is often made after a trial of asthma medications.
Young children may not describe chest tightness or shortness of breath; parents report night cough, exercise intolerance, or recurrent 'chest colds' instead.
Obesity can cause dyspnea and exercise limitation that mimic asthma; symptoms may be less responsive to standard asthma therapy.

general.mild: Comfortable, playful, speaking in full sentences; no distress at rest
general.moderate: Mildly anxious, prefers sitting upright, speaks in short phrases, mild tachypnea
general.severe: Anxious and agitated, sitting upright and leaning forward, speaks in single words, using accessory muscles
general.critical: Lethargic or exhausted, unable to speak or feed, may be confused or have decreased responsiveness

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all lung fields during quiet breathing, then ask the child to breathe deeply
findings.finding: Diffuse expiratory wheezing, often polyphonic and worse on expiration

findings.maneuver: Listen to the ratio of inspiration to expiration over the trachea and chest
Observe the child's breathing at rest, looking at the neck, intercostal spaces, and abdomen
findings.finding: Use of accessory muscles, suprasternal or intercostal retractions, nasal flaring

findings.maneuver: Count the respiratory rate for a full minute while the child is calm
findings.finding: Respiratory rate above the normal range for age

findings.maneuver: Ask the child to speak a full sentence or count to ten in one breath
findings.finding: Speaks in short phrases or single words only
Minimal or absent breath sounds with a quiet chest despite severe distress

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, tongue, and nail beds in good light
Assess alertness, orientation, and response to voice or touch
Inspect the face and under-eye area
findings.finding: Dark circles under the eyes (allergic shiners)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the nasal mucosa with a light
findings.finding: Pale, boggy nasal mucosa with clear discharge, consistent with allergic rhinitis

findings.maneuver: Inspect the flexural creases, cheeks, and extensor surfaces
Measure the temperature and ask about recent fever
Auscultate for focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds
findings.finding: No focal crackles, dullness, or bronchial breath sounds

findings.maneuver: Listen over the neck and trachea during quiet breathing
Inspect the fingertips and nail beds
Compare breath sounds side to side
findings.finding: Symmetric breath sounds without focal decrease

labs.caveat: Mild peripheral eosinophilia supports an atopic phenotype but is neither sensitive nor specific; a normal value does not argue against asthma.
Usually normal in asthma; a marked elevation should prompt consideration of pneumonia or another infection.
Mild leukocytosis can occur with viral triggers or systemic corticosteroids; it does not indicate bacterial infection by itself.
Only relevant in a severe or life-threatening exacerbation; early in an attack the pH may be normal or respiratory alkalosis may be present.
A normal or rising PaCO2 during a severe attack signals fatigue and impending respiratory failure.

findings.finding: Right axis deviation or right atrial enlargement in chronic severe disease

findings.text: Normal or hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms
Peribronchial cuffing or increased perihilar markings
No focal consolidation, effusion, or pneumothorax

initial.why: Confirms reversible airflow obstruction and is the primary diagnostic test in children old enough to perform it (generally about 5–6 years and older)
Objective measure of airflow obstruction when spirometry is not available; useful for monitoring and for assessing severity during an exacerbation
Assesses oxygenation during an exacerbation and guides severity classification
Not routine; helps exclude pneumonia, pneumothorax, or foreign body
initial.only_if: the presentation is atypical, there is fever or focal findings, or a complication or alternative diagnosis is suspected

confirmatory.why: Demonstrates an obstructive pattern with a significant improvement after a short-acting bronchodilator, confirming reversible airway obstruction

supporting.test: Allergy skin testing or allergen-specific IgE
supporting.why: Identifies allergic triggers and supports an atopic phenotype; helps guide trigger avoidance
supporting.only_if: an allergic trigger is suspected or the history suggests atopy

supporting.why: Demonstrates airway hyperresponsiveness when spirometry is normal but asthma is still suspected
supporting.only_if: symptoms are consistent with asthma but baseline spirometry is normal

supporting.why: Noninvasive marker of eosinophilic airway inflammation that can support the diagnosis and guide therapy
supporting.only_if: the diagnosis is uncertain or adherence and control are being assessed

not_indicated.why: Routine blood counts do not establish the diagnosis and are not needed in a typical presentation
Not useful for diagnosing asthma; reserve for suspected infection
No role in asthma; consider only when bacterial pneumonia is a serious concern
No role in the evaluation of pediatric wheeze
Not routinely needed; obtain only if the child is dehydrated, on high-dose corticosteroids, or has an electrolyte concern
Not routine in a classic presentation; does not diagnose asthma and adds radiation exposure

decision_points: Spirometry is the preferred confirmatory test but is generally not feasible before about age 5–6; in younger children the diagnosis is supported by a documented response to a trial of asthma medication and by excluding alternative causes
A normal chest x-ray does not exclude asthma; order it to look for complications or alternative diagnoses, not to confirm asthma
Consider a trial of short-acting bronchodilator and inhaled corticosteroid in young children who cannot perform spirometry, with reassessment after 4–6 weeks
Assess severity and control at every visit using symptom frequency, nighttime awakenings, rescue inhaler use, and activity limitation
In a severe exacerbation, a normal or rising PaCO2 is a warning sign of impending respiratory failure

criteria.name: Clinical diagnosis of asthma in children
criteria.summary: The diagnosis is clinical, based on a history of recurrent or persistent wheeze, cough, chest tightness, or shortness of breath that is variable over time and worse at night or with common triggers such as viral infections, exercise, cold air, or allergens, together with documented reversible airflow obstruction or a clear response to asthma therapy, after alternative diagnoses have been considered.

differential.name: Bronchiolitis
differential.why_considered: Wheezing and respiratory distress in a young child, often after a viral illness

history: Age under 2 years, usually 2–6 months
Preceded by 1–3 days of clear rhinorrhea and low-grade fever
First episode rather than recurrent episodes
Winter or early spring season
exam: Fine crackles or rales in addition to wheeze
Wheeze may be diffuse but often asymmetric
labs: Respiratory viral panel positive for RSV, rhinovirus, or other virus
imaging: Chest x-ray may show hyperinflation, peribronchial cuffing, or atelectasis; not required for diagnosis

differential.name: Foreign body aspiration
differential.why_considered: Sudden onset of cough, wheeze, or respiratory distress in a toddler
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset of symptoms while eating, playing with small objects, or with no preceding illness

history: Sudden onset, often while eating or playing
Choking episode witnessed or suspected
Symptoms unilateral or persistent despite bronchodilator therapy
No prior history of recurrent wheeze
exam: Unilateral wheeze or decreased breath sounds
Stridor if the object is in the upper airway
imaging: Radio-opaque foreign body on chest x-ray
Unilateral hyperinflation or mediastinal shift on expiratory film
Air trapping on the affected side

differential.name: Pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Cough, tachypnea, and respiratory distress in a child

history: Fever is prominent
Acute onset over days rather than recurrent episodes
Productive cough with purulent sputum
No history of recurrent wheeze or atopy
exam: Focal crackles, dullness to percussion, or bronchial breath sounds
imaging: Focal consolidation or infiltrate on chest x-ray

differential.name: Cystic fibrosis
differential.why_considered: Recurrent wheeze, cough, and respiratory infections in a child
differential.trigger: Failure to thrive, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, or persistent GI symptoms in a child with wheeze

history: Failure to thrive or poor weight gain
Recurrent sinus or pulmonary infections
Steatorrhea, bulky foul-smelling stools
Salty-tasting skin
Family history of cystic fibrosis
labs: Elevated sweat chloride on sweat chloride test
Pancreatic insufficiency with low fecal elastase
imaging: Chest x-ray with bronchiectasis, hyperinflation, or mucus plugging

differential.name: Vocal cord dysfunction
differential.why_considered: Dyspnea and noisy breathing that can mimic asthma, especially in adolescents

history: Symptoms occur at rest or with stress, not primarily with exercise or allergens
No nighttime cough or nocturnal awakenings
Symptoms may be triggered by strong odors or emotional stress
Poor response to asthma medications
exam: Wheeze heard loudest over the neck rather than the chest
Symptoms may resolve with distraction or during sleep
labs: Normal spirometry or flow-volume loop showing inspiratory flattening
imaging: Laryngoscopy showing paradoxical vocal cord adduction during inspiration

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough and wheeze in a child, often worse at night

history: Cough or wheeze after feeding or when lying flat
Frequent spitting up or vomiting in infants
Heartburn or sour taste in older children
No clear response to bronchodilators
exam: May have poor weight gain in infants
labs: pH probe or impedance study showing reflux episodes
imaging: Upper GI series may show reflux or anatomic abnormality

differential.name: Allergic rhinitis
differential.why_considered: Chronic nasal congestion, cough, and wheeze in an atopic child

history: Prominent nasal congestion, sneezing, and itchy watery eyes
Symptoms seasonal or with allergen exposure
Cough often from postnasal drip rather than bronchospasm
No nighttime awakenings from wheeze
exam: Pale, boggy nasal mucosa with clear discharge
labs: Positive allergy skin testing or specific IgE

differential.name: Congenital heart disease with left-to-right shunt
differential.why_considered: Tachypnea, poor feeding, and respiratory distress in an infant
differential.trigger: Poor feeding, failure to thrive, or a cardiac murmur in an infant with respiratory symptoms

history: Symptoms present since birth or early infancy
Poor feeding and sweating with feeds
Failure to thrive
No symptom-free intervals
exam: Bounding pulses or wide pulse pressure
labs: Brain natriuretic peptide may be elevated
imaging: Cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings on chest x-ray

severity.mild: Symptoms less than twice a week, nighttime awakenings less than twice a month, no activity limitation, FEV1 at or above 80% predicted, and symptoms controlled with as-needed short-acting bronchodilator alone
severity.moderate: Symptoms more than twice a week but not daily, nighttime awakenings 3–4 times a month, some activity limitation, FEV1 60–80% predicted, and requiring daily controller therapy
severity.severe: Symptoms throughout the day, nighttime awakenings more than once a week, significant activity limitation, FEV1 below 60% predicted, and requiring high-dose controller therapy plus consideration of biologic therapy
severity.critical: Life-threatening exacerbation with inability to speak or feed, silent chest, cyanosis, altered mental status, or impending respiratory failure requiring ICU admission and possible mechanical ventilation

red_flags.meaning: Airflow is so limited that breath sounds are barely audible; impending respiratory failure

red_flags.finding: Cyanosis of lips, tongue, or nail beds
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypoxemia; needs immediate oxygen and emergency treatment
Hypoxemia or hypercapnia; impending respiratory failure

red_flags.finding: Inability to speak in full sentences or feed
red_flags.meaning: Severe exacerbation; indicates significant airflow obstruction

red_flags.finding: Use of accessory muscles, retractions, or nasal flaring
red_flags.meaning: Increased work of breathing; moderate to severe exacerbation

red_flags.finding: Respiratory rate above the normal range for age with fatigue
red_flags.meaning: Exhaustion; may progress to respiratory failure

red_flags.finding: Normal or rising PaCO2 during a severe attack
red_flags.meaning: The child is tiring and can no longer hyperventilate; impending respiratory failure

complications.name: Status asthmaticus
clues: Severe exacerbation not responding to repeated bronchodilator treatments

complications.name: Growth impairment or poor school performance
clues: Poor weight gain in young children

complications.name: Airway remodeling with fixed airflow obstruction

special_populations.differences: May present with feeding difficulty, rapid breathing, or coughing during feeds rather than classic wheezing; diagnosis is often made after a trial of asthma medications because spirometry is not feasible.

Young children may not describe chest tightness or shortness of breath; parents report night cough, exercise intolerance, or recurrent chest colds instead. Spirometry is generally feasible after age 5–6.
Obesity can cause dyspnea and exercise limitation that mimic asthma; symptoms may be less responsive to standard asthma therapy and require weight management as part of care.
Asthma may improve, worsen, or remain unchanged during pregnancy; poor control increases the risk of preterm birth and low birth weight, so controller therapy should be continued.

key_questions.question: How often does your child have wheezing, cough, or trouble breathing, and how often does it wake them at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent episodes over weeks to months with nighttime or early-morning symptoms; frequency and nighttime awakenings define severity and control

key_questions.question: What seems to set it off or make it worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Viral colds, exercise, cold air, pets, dust, mold, pollen, smoke, or strong odors; identifiable triggers support asthma

key_questions.question: Does your child get completely better between episodes, or are the symptoms always there?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptom-free intervals with episodic flares; continuous symptoms since birth suggest another diagnosis

key_questions.question: Does the breathing trouble get better with a rescue inhaler or nebulizer?
key_questions.looking_for: Documented improvement with albuterol supports reversible airflow obstruction

key_questions.question: How long has this been going on, and how many episodes has your child had?
key_questions.looking_for: Months to years of recurrent episodes rather than a single acute illness

key_questions.question: Can your child keep up with other kids when playing or running?
key_questions.looking_for: Exercise intolerance or stopping to catch their breath; activity limitation indicates poor control

key_questions.question: Has your child ever had a choking episode or sudden onset of coughing while eating or playing with small objects?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset with choking suggests foreign body aspiration, not asthma

key_questions.question: Has your child had fever, weight loss, night sweats, or a cough bringing up blood or colored sputum?
key_questions.looking_for: These argue against asthma and raise concern for pneumonia, tuberculosis, or another chronic illness

key_questions.question: Does your child have eczema, hay fever, or food allergies?
key_questions.looking_for: Personal atopic history supports an asthma phenotype

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family have asthma, allergies, or eczema?
key_questions.looking_for: Parental or sibling asthma, especially maternal, is a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Does anyone smoke in the home or in a car your child rides in?
key_questions.looking_for: Secondhand smoke exposure is a common, modifiable trigger

key_questions.question: What medicines has your child tried, and how often do they use the rescue inhaler in a typical week?
key_questions.looking_for: Rescue inhaler use more than twice a week, or a prior controller trial, informs severity and diagnosis

key_questions.question: Any known allergies to medicines, foods, or environmental allergens?
key_questions.looking_for: Allergic triggers and any prior reaction to asthma medications

key_questions.question: Does your child have trouble feeding, or do they cough or sweat during feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: In infants, feeding difficulty or sweating with feeds may be the presenting symptom

key_questions.question: Has your child been growing and gaining weight normally?
key_questions.looking_for: Failure to thrive raises concern for cystic fibrosis or congenital heart disease

reasoning_points: Recurrent, variable wheeze, cough, chest tightness, or shortness of breath over weeks to months, worse at night or early morning
Symptoms provoked by typical triggers such as viral infections, exercise, cold air, allergens, or smoke, with symptom-free intervals between episodes
Documented improvement with a short-acting bronchodilator, or a clear response to a trial of asthma therapy in a child too young for spirometry
Spirometry showing an obstructive pattern with significant reversibility after bronchodilator in a child old enough to perform the test
Supporting atopic features such as eczema, allergic rhinitis, or a family history of asthma or atopy
Alternative diagnoses considered and excluded, including bronchiolitis, foreign body aspiration, pneumonia, cystic fibrosis, vocal cord dysfunction, and congenital heart disease
Severity and control assessed from symptom frequency, nighttime awakenings, rescue inhaler use, and activity limitation

easy: School-age child with recurrent nighttime cough and wheeze that improves with albuterol
Known eczema and allergic rhinitis with a parent who has asthma
Symptoms clearly triggered by exercise and cold air
medium: Toddler with recurrent 'chest colds' and no wheeze heard in the office
Child whose only symptom is chronic cough, worse at night
Symptoms attributed to poor inhaler technique or nonadherence
Coexisting allergic rhinitis or obesity muddying the picture
hard: Infant with feeding difficulty and tachypnea, too young for spirometry, diagnosed after a medication trial
Sudden unilateral wheeze in a toddler suggesting foreign body aspiration
Adolescent with exertional dyspnea and noisy breathing that is actually vocal cord dysfunction
Child with failure to thrive and recurrent infections suggesting cystic fibrosis
Severe exacerbation with a quiet chest, cyanosis, or drowsiness
